plan.topic_summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) is the set of techniques used to protect quantum information from decoherence and gate errors, and is widely regarded as a prerequisite for fault-tolerant quantum computing. For a 1–5 year view, the central question is whether logical qubit performance will improve rapidly enough to enable commercially useful algorithms, and which code architectures and hardware modalities will dominate.
key_questions: What is the current state of logical qubit performance across leading hardware modalities, and are any platforms demonstrating a clear advantage of logical over physical qubits in practical tasks?
Which QEC code architectures are converging as the dominant approach, and what are the estimated resource overheads (physical qubits per logical qubit) for commercially useful algorithms?
What are the key engineering bottlenecks—hardware yield, control electronics, cryogenic integration, measurement latency—preventing scale-up of QEC systems beyond small logical qubit counts?
What is the realistic timeline to a fault-tolerant quantum computer capable of running a commercially useful algorithm, and what milestones would indicate progress or stalling?

Could alternative strategies such as error mitigation, approximate QEC, or new code families reduce the resource requirements enough to make useful quantum advantage achievable before full fault tolerance is reached?

gaps: Evidence is heavily weighted toward superconducting surface-code and bosonic GKP platforms; trapped-ion, neutral-atom, and photonic QEC progress is underrepresented in the science findings (only R4 touches trapped ions, M4 touches photonics).

The 'beyond break-even' results (S1, S2, S4) demonstrate logical memory lifetime exceeding physical qubit lifetime, but the gap to full fault-tolerant computation (arbitrary circuits, logical gates) is not directly addressed by any single finding; the report must be careful not to overstate readiness.
Decoder performance at large code distances (d≥9) is not well characterized; S2 gives 63 µs latency at d=5 but no data at the distances needed for practical fault tolerance.

Most overhead-reduction and alternative-code results (R3, R5, S7) are simulation-based or extrapolated, not hardware-validated; this is noted in the findings but the report should make the simulation-to-hardware gap explicit.
X findings are all unverified social signals and cannot be used as factual evidence in the report.

sources.title: Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold
sources.abstract: Quantum error correction [1, 2, 3, 4] provides a path to reach practical quantum computing by combining multiple physical qubits into a logical qubit, where the logical error rate is suppressed exponentially as more qubits are added. However, this exponential suppression only occurs if the physical error rate is below a critical threshold. Here, we present two below-threshold surface code memories on our newest generation of superconducting processors, Willow: a distance-7 code, and a distance-5 code integrated with a real-time decoder. The logical error rate of our larger quantum memory is suppressed by a factor of $$\varLambda \mathrm{=2.14}\pm 0.02$$ when increasing the code distance by two, culminating in a 101-qubit distance-7 code with 0.143% ± 0.003% error per cycle of error correction. This logical memory is also beyond break-even, exceeding its best physical qubit’s lifetime by a factor of $$2.4\pm 0.3$$ . Our system maintains below-threshold performance when decoding in real time, achieving an average decoder latency of 63 μs at distance-5 up to a million cycles, with a cycle time of 1.1 μs. We also run repetition codes up to distance-29 and find that logical performance is limited by rare correlated error events occurring approximately once every hour, or $$3$$ $$\times $$ $${10}^{9}$$ cycles. Our results present device performance that, if scaled, could realize the operational requirements of large scale fault-tolerant quantum algorithms.

sources.title: Quantum Error Correction in Quaternionic Hilbert Spaces
sources.abstract: We propose quaternion-based strategies for quantum error correction by extending quantum mechanics into quaternionic Hilbert spaces. Building on the properties of quaternionic quantum states, we define quaternionic analogues of Pauli operators and quantum gates, ensuring inner product preservation and Hilbert space conditions. A simple encoding scheme maps logical qubits into quaternionic systems, introducing natural redundancy and enhanced resilience against noise. We construct a quaternionic extension of the five-qubit code, introducing a framework of 15 syndrome measurements to detect quaternionic errors, including quaternionically rotated error components. Numerical estimates show that the quaternionic five-qubit code achieves a logical error threshold of approximately $p_{th} \approx 0.015$, demonstrating improved performance compared to the standard complex-valued code. These results suggest a new pathway for quantum error correction in high-noise environments, leveraging the richer structure of quaternionic quantum mechanics to improve fault tolerance.

sources.title: Overcoming leakage in quantum error correction
sources.abstract: Abstract The leakage of quantum information out of the two computational states of a qubit into other energy states represents a major challenge for quantum error correction. During the operation of an error-corrected algorithm, leakage builds over time and spreads through multi-qubit interactions. This leads to correlated errors that degrade the exponential suppression of the logical error with scale, thus challenging the feasibility of quantum error correction as a path towards fault-tolerant quantum computation. Here, we demonstrate a distance-3 surface code and distance-21 bit-flip code on a quantum processor for which leakage is removed from all qubits in each cycle. This shortens the lifetime of leakage and curtails its ability to spread and induce correlated errors. We report a tenfold reduction in the steady-state leakage population of the data qubits encoding the logical state and an average leakage population of less than 1 × 10 −3 throughout the entire device. Our leakage removal process efficiently returns the system back to the computational basis. Adding it to a code circuit would prevent leakage from inducing correlated error across cycles. With this demonstration that leakage can be contained, we have resolved a key challenge for practical quantum error correction at scale.

sources.title: Thermodynamic Recycling of Algorithmic Failure Branches: Quantum-Computer Demonstration with Quantum Error Correction
sources.abstract: Thermodynamic trade-off relations dictate fundamental limits on the performance of thermodynamic tasks through costs such as heat dissipation. Here, we propose a framework called thermodynamic recycling to circumvent these limits in quantum processors by exploiting failure branches of quantum algorithms, which are usually discarded. The key component is an athermal bath naturally generated during the resetting of a failure branch. By coupling this bath to a target system prior to relaxation, thermodynamic tasks can be performed beyond conventional thermodynamic limits. We apply this framework to information erasure and derive the reduction in heat dissipation analytically. As a demonstration, we implement our framework on IBM's superconducting quantum processor by combining the Harrow--Hassidim--Lloyd algorithm with three-qubit quantum error correction, thereby reducing the heat dissipated in erasing syndrome information. Despite substantial noise and errors in current hardware, our method achieves erasure with heat dissipation below the Landauer limit. This work establishes an operational connection between quantum computing and quantum thermodynamics for resource-efficient quantum computation.

sources.title: Real-time quantum error correction beyond break-even
Sparse Mamba Decoder for Quantum Error Correction: Efficient Defect-Centric Processing of Surface Code Syndromes
sources.abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is essential for building fault-tolerant quantum computers, requiring decoders that are simultaneously accurate, fast, and scalable. Most state-of-the-art neural decoders achieve high accuracy but process the full dense syndrome array of size $O(d^2 R) $regardless of the actual error rate, where d is the code distance and R is the number of measurement rounds. At physically relevant error rates (p ~ 0.1%), fewer than 5% of syndrome entries contain active detection events -- yet existing decoders process the entire syndrome volume. We introduce the Sparse Mamba Decoder (SMD), a defect-centric neural decoder that processes only the k active detection events using a 13-dimensional feature representation per defect and a Mamba state-space backbone, achieving $O(k)$ complexity. Across depolarizing, uniform circuit-level, SI1000, and Google Sycamore experimental benchmarks, SMD reduces the MWPM logical error rate by up to 49% at $d \le 5$ under SI1000 noise, runs 95-467x faster than the Tesseract near-MLD decoder and 232-463x faster than Belief Matching, and maintains nearly constant latency (24-57 us) across d = 3-9 under uniform circuit-level noise. On the Sycamore experimental dataset, the SMD ensemble matches or slightly surpasses the dense Mamba decoder of Varbanov et al. All results are obtained on commodity NVIDIA GPUs with 7.5-16M parameters, without specialized accelerators.

sources.title: Quantum Error Correction with Quantum Autoencoders
sources.abstract: Active quantum error correction is a central ingredient to achieve robust quantum processors. In this paper we investigate the potential of quantum machine learning for quantum error correction in a quantum memory. Specifically, we demonstrate how quantum neural networks, in the form of quantum autoencoders, can be trained to learn optimal strategies for active detection and correction of errors, including spatially correlated computational errors as well as qubit losses. We highlight that the denoising capabilities of quantum autoencoders are not limited to the protection of specific states but extend to the entire logical codespace. We also show that quantum neural networks can be used to discover new logical encodings that are optimally adapted to the underlying noise. Moreover, we find that, even in the presence of moderate noise in the quantum autoencoders themselves, they may still be successfully used to perform beneficial quantum error correction and thereby extend the lifetime of a logical qubit.

sources.title: Systematic Approach to Hyperbolic Quantum Error Correction Codes
sources.abstract: Quantum error correction codes defined on hyperbolic lattices leverage the unique geometric properties of the hyperbolic space to enhance the performance of quantum error correction. By embedding qubits in hyperbolic lattices, these codes achieve higher encoding rates and lower qubit overhead compared to those defined on conventional Euclidean lattices. Building on recent advances in hyperbolic crystallography, we introduce a unified framework for the systematic construction and scalable benchmarking of CSS quantum error correction codes on hyperbolic lattices. A central component of this framework is the Hyperbolic Cycle Basis algorithm, which employs graph-theoretic methods to efficiently identify all plaquette cycles (parity-check supports) and nontrivial cycles (logical operators). This enables scalable and automated benchmarking of a broad class of CSS codes defined on hyperbolic geometries. We apply this framework to construct and simulate two representative hyperbolic quantum error correction codes (HQECCs), evaluating key performance metrics such as encoding rate, error threshold, and code distance for different sublattices. While HQECCs serve as concrete examples, the framework can be adapted to a wide range of CSS codes, including those with more intricate stabilizer structures such as Floquet codes. This work establishes a foundation for systematic exploration and benchmarking of CSS codes on hyperbolic lattices, paving the way toward practical, high-performance quantum error correction.

sources.title: Quantum Error Correction For Dummies
sources.venue: IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)
sources.abstract: In the current Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) era of quantum computing, qubit technologies are prone to imperfections, giving rise to various errors such as gate errors, decoherence/dephasing, measurement errors, leakage, and crosstalk. These errors present challenges in achieving error-free computation within NISQ devices. A proposed solution to this issue is Quantum Error Correction (QEC), which aims to rectify the corrupted qubit state through a three-step process: (i) detection: identifying the presence of an error, (ii) decoding: pinpointing the location(s) of the affected qubit(s), and (iii) correction: restoring the faulty qubits to their original states. QEC is an expanding field of research that encompasses intricate concepts. In this paper, we aim to provide a comprehensive review of the historical context, current state, and future prospects of Quantum Error Correction, tailored to cater to computer scientists with limited familiarity with quantum physics and its associated mathematical concepts. In this work, we, (a) explain the foundational principles of QEC and explore existing Quantum Error Correction Codes (QECC) designed to correct errors in qubits, (b) explore the practicality of these QECCs with regard to implementation and error correction quality, and (c) highlight the challenges associated with implementing QEC within the context of the current landscape of NISQ computers.

sources.title: Quantum error correction of qudits beyond break-even
sources.abstract: Hilbert space dimension is a key resource for quantum information processing1,2. Not only is a large overall Hilbert space an essential requirement for quantum error correction, but a large local Hilbert space can also be advantageous for realizing gates and algorithms more efficiently3–7. As a result, there has been considerable experimental effort in recent years to develop quantum computing platforms using qudits (d-dimensional quantum systems with d > 2) as the fundamental unit of quantum information8–19. Just as with qubits, quantum error correction of these qudits will be necessary in the long run, but so far, error correction of logical qudits has not been demonstrated experimentally. Here we report the experimental realization of an error-corrected logical qutrit (d = 3) and ququart (d = 4), which was achieved with the Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill bosonic code20. Using a reinforcement learning agent21,22, we optimized the Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill qutrit (ququart) as a ternary (quaternary) quantum memory and achieved beyond break-even error correction with a gain of 1.82 ± 0.03 (1.87 ± 0.03). This work represents a novel way of leveraging the large Hilbert space of a harmonic oscillator to realize hardware-efficient quantum error correction. Quantum error correction of a logical qutrit and ququart were experimentally realized beyond the break-even point with the Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill bosonic code.

sources.title: Approximate quantum error correction theory of non-isometric codes
sources.abstract: Non-isometric encoding arises in various important contexts in quantum error correction, most notably in the finite-energy, non-ideal codewords inevitable in experimental realizations of continuous-variable codes, and holographic quantum gravity. In this work, we present a general and systematic theory of non-isometric quantum error-correcting codes. In particular, we employ the approximate quantum error correction framework to quantitatively study the fundamental limitations imposed by non-isometric encodings on the accuracy of quantum error correction and implementation of logical operations. We apply our theory to analyze GKP and tiger codes under energy constraints, and discuss the implications to holography.

sources.title: Introduction to quantum error correction and fault tolerance
sources.abstract: These lecture notes from the 2019 Les Houches Summer School on “Quantum Information Machines” are intended to provide an introduction to classical and quantum error correction with bits and qubits, and with continuous variable systems (harmonic oscillators). The focus on the latter will be on practical examples that can be realized today or in the near future with a modular architecture based on superconducting electrical circuits and microwave photons. The goal and vision is “hardware-efficient” quantum error correction that does not require exponentially large hardware overhead in order to achieve practical and useful levels of fault tolerance and circuit depth.

sources.title: Error Correction Is a Landauer Machine: The Thermodynamic Floor of Quantum Error-Correction Overhead
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: Quantum error correction is priced in combinatorial currency — rate, distance, threshold — while the physical cost of performing correction goes uncounted. Every cycle of active (measurement-based) error correction erases information: syndrome extraction, majority voting, and ancilla re-initialization each reset redundancy, and Landauer's principle prices each erasure at no less than kT·ln2 per bit. This paper derives the resulting thermodynamic floor for correction overhead — (n−k)/k · kT·ln2 per logical qubit per round for an [[n,k]] code — verifies its scaling across code families (linear for repetition, quadratic for surface, constant for constant-rate), and applies the JPCUB joules-per-correct-answer metric to rank correction architectures. A two-level nested (tree-structured) code is compared with flat Hamming codes of equal rate on a clustered NAND-like channel: hierarchical decoding cuts the per-round erasure count by a factor of 1.6 to 3, while the naive construction pays a residual-error penalty — a partial null that leaves the floor claim intact and defines the protocol for an industrial flash-memory test. Biological systems that run robust quantum processes without correction (photosynthetic energy transfer, radical-pair magnetoreception) show the floor is an architecture choice: structure prepays in capital energy what correction pays in operating erasures. Autonomous and dissipative correction is identified as the boundary of the claim.

sources.title: Reducing quantum error correction overhead using soft information
sources.abstract: Imperfect measurements are a prevalent source of error across quantum computing platforms, significantly degrading the logical error rates achievable on current hardware. To mitigate this issue, rich measurement data referred to as soft information has been proposed to efficiently identify and correct measurement errors as they occur. In this work, we model soft information decoding across a variety of physical qubit platforms and decoders and showcase how soft information can make error correction viable at lower code distances and higher physical error rates than is otherwise possible. We simulate the effects of soft information decoding on quantum memories for surface codes and bivariate bicycle codes, and evaluate the error suppression performance of soft decoders against traditional decoders. Our simulations show that soft information decoding on near-term devices can provide up to 11% higher error suppression on superconducting qubits and up to 20% stronger error suppression on neutral atom qubits. These accuracy gains correspond to 13% and 33% reductions in the physical qubit footprint of superconducting and neutral atom devices respectively when operating at a logical error rate of $10^{-6}$, showcasing that soft information is a powerful tool for reducing the cost and complexity of large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computers.

sources.title: Reducing Quantum Error Correction Overhead with Versatile Flag-Sharing Syndrome Extraction Circuits
sources.venue: IEEE Transactions on Quantum Engineering, vol. 6, pp. 1-24, 2025, Art no. 3101524
sources.abstract: Given that quantum error correction processes are unreliable, an efficient error syndrome extraction circuit should use fewer ancillary qubits, quantum gates, and measurements, while maintaining low circuit depth, to minimizing the circuit area, roughly defined as the product of circuit depth and the number of physical qubits. We propose to design parallel flagged syndrome extraction with shared flag qubits for quantum stabilizer codes. Versatile parallelization techniques are employed to minimize the required circuit area, thereby improving the error threshold and overall performance. Specifically, all the measurement outcomes in multiple rounds of syndrome extraction are integrated into a lookup table decoder, allowing us to parallelize multiple stabilizer measurements with shared flag qubits. We present flag-sharing and fully parallel schemes for the [[17,1,5]] and [[19,1,5]] Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes. This methodology extends to the [[5,1,3]] non-CSS code, achieving the minimum known circuit area. Numerical simulations have demonstrated improved pseudothresholds for these codes by up to an order of magnitude compared to previous schemes in the literature.

sources.title: A simple universal routing strategy for reducing the connectivity requirements of quantum LDPC codes
sources.abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check codes reduce quantum error correction overhead but require dense, long-range connectivity that challenges hardware implementation, particularly for superconducting processors. We address this problem by demonstrating that long-range connections can be reduced at the cost of increased syndrome extraction circuit depth. Our approach is based on the observation that X and Z ancilla qubits form short loops with data qubits - a property that holds for any quantum code. This enables implementing stabilizer measurement circuits by routing data qubit information through ancilla qubits when direct connections are unavailable. For bivariate bicycle codes, we remove up to 50% of long-range connections while approximately doubling the circuit depth, with the circuit-level distance remaining largely preserved. This method can also be applied to surface codes, achieving the same hexagonal connectivity requirement as McEwen et al. (Quantum 7, 1172 (2023)). Our routing approach for designing syndrome extraction circuits is applicable to diverse quantum codes, offering a practical pathway toward their implementation on hardware with connectivity constraints.

sources.title: Performance Analysis for Crosstalk Errors between Parallel Entangling Gates in Trapped Ion Quantum Error Correction
sources.abstract: The ability to execute a large number of quantum gates in parallel is a fundamental requirement for quantum error correction, allowing an error threshold to exist under the finite coherence time of physical qubits. Recently, two-dimensional ion crystals have been demonstrated as a plausible approach to scale up the qubit number in a trapped ion quantum computer. However, although the long-range Coulomb interaction between the ions enables their strong connectivity, it also complicates the design of parallel gates and leads to intrinsic crosstalk errors. Here we examine the effects of crosstalk errors on a rotated surface code. We show that, instead of the distance-3 code considered in previous works, a distance-5 code is necessary to correct the two-qubit crosstalk error. We numerically calculate the logical error rates and coherence times under various crosstalk errors, gate infidelities and coherence times of the physical qubits, and we optimize the parallelism level according to the competition between different error sources. We show that a break-even point can be reached under realistic parameters. We further analyze the spatial dependence of the crosstalk, and discuss the scaling of the logical error rate versus the code distance for the long-term goal of a logical error rate below $10^{-10}$.

sources.title: Surface-Code Overhead Tech4Biz Solutions A Lightweight, Exact, and Reproducible Calculator for Surface-Code Quantum Error Correction Overhead
Suppression of Universal Errors in DFS-Encoded Superconducting Geometric Logical \emph{T} Gate
sources.abstract: High-fidelity logical \emph{T}-gate realization constitutes a core prerequisite for large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing. However, conventional magic state distillation requires massive physical qubit overhead across successive distillation rounds, alongside sophisticated measurement and feedback control, thereby inducing considerable spatial and temporal resource consumption. Herein, we propose a controlled superconducting geometric logical \emph{T} gate scheme that achieves high-order suppression of universal errors, by integrating decoherence-free subspace encoding with multi-loop optimized composite geometric pulse engineering. Guided by tailored trajectory design, we systematically establish unified gate construction frameworks for conventional geometric, composite geometric, and optimized composite geometric protocols. By flexibly controling additional parametric degrees of freedom, the proposed scheme achieves substantially enhanced robustness against diverse noise sources. Numerical simulations reveal that, within tunable superconducting quantum circuits, our geometric logical \emph{T} gate outperforms both conventional composite geometric and dynamical gates in suppressing Rabi frequency, detuning, and residual inter-qubit crosstalk errors that can all be suppressed to the fourth order, while additionally providing inherent suppression of collective dephasing errors. The present strategy alleviates intrinsic limitations of mainstream approaches and opens a promising avenue toward robust high-fidelity logical \emph{T} gate construction.

sources.title: Demonstration of low-overhead quantum error correction codes
Decoherence rate in random Lindblad dynamics
sources.abstract: Open quantum systems undergo decoherence, which is responsible for the transition from quantum to classical behavior. The time scale in which decoherence takes place can be analyzed using upper limits to its rate. We examine the dynamics of open chaotic quantum systems governed by random Lindblad operators sourced from Gaussian and Ginibre ensembles with Wigner-Dyson symmetry classes. In these systems, the ensemble-averaged purity decays monotonically as a function of time. This decay is governed by the decoherence rate, which is upper-bounded by the dimension of their Hilbert space and is independent of the ensemble symmetry. These findings hold upon mixing different ensembles, indicating the universal character of the decoherence rate limit. Moreover, our findings reveal that open chaotic quantum systems governed by random Lindbladians tend to exhibit the most rapid decoherence, regardless of the initial state. This phenomenon is associated with the concentration of the decoherence rate near its upper bound. Our work identifies primary features of decoherence in dissipative quantum chaos, with applications ranging from quantum foundations to high-energy physics and quantum technologies.

sources.title: Quantum error correction at ultra-low overhead
sources.abstract: Suppressing errors is the central challenge for useful large-scale quantum computing. While quantum error correction promises a viable solution to this challenge, existing codes typically suffer from trade-offs among encoding efficiency, error threshold, and hardware feasibility. Here, we introduce Cornucopia codes, a family of practical, hardware-efficient quantum low-density parity-check codes that achieve an ultra-high encoding rate exceeding $1/2$ while maintaining a pseudo-threshold exceeding $0.4\%$ under the standard circuit-level noise model. Inspired by recent affine-permutation-based code constructions and the long-range connectivity available in reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays, we adopt a structured code geometry in which the code layout, atom rearrangement, and syndrome-extraction schedule are co-designed. This structure enables nonlocal syndrome measurements through simple, parallel atom rearrangements. A complete syndrome extraction cycle measures all $X$- and $Z$-type checks in parallel with $12$ entangling layers, independent of the code size. The resulting threshold is comparable to those of the surface code and bivariate bicycle codes. In particular, a single code block $[[2844,1426,18]]$ encodes $1{,}426$ distance-$18$ logical qubits, achieving an extrapolated logical error rate of $2.6\times10^{-16}$ ($1.9\times10^{-31}$) per logical qubit per cycle, assuming the physical error rate of $0.1\%$ ($0.01\%$). By comparison, a bivariate bicycle code implementation would require more than $68{,}000$ physical qubits to encode the same number of logical qubits at a comparable logical error rate. These results bring demonstrations of ultra-low-overhead quantum error correction within the reach of near-term quantum processors.

sources.title: A lower bound on the overhead of quantum error correction in low dimensions
sources.abstract: We show that a quantum architecture with an error correction procedure limited to geometrically local operations incurs an overhead that grows with the system size, even if arbitrary error-free classical computation is allowed. In particular, we prove that in order to operate a quantum error correcting code in 2D at a logical error rate of $δ$, a space overhead of $Ω(\sqrt{\log(1/δ)})$ is needed for any constant depolarizing noise $p > 0$.

sources.title: Quantum Prometheus: Defying Overhead with Recycled Ancillas in Quantum Error Correction
sources.venue: International Symposium on Quality Electronic Design (ISQED)
sources.abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is crucial for ensuring the reliability of quantum computers. However, implementing QEC often requires a significant number of qubits, leading to substantial overhead. One of the major challenges in quantum computing is reducing this overhead, especially since QEC codes depend heavily on ancilla qubits for stabilizer measurements. In this work, we propose reducing the number of ancilla qubits by reusing the same ancilla qubits for both X-and Z-type stabilizers. This is achieved by alternating between X and Z stabilizer measurements during each half-round, cutting the number of required ancilla qubits in half. This technique can be applied broadly across various QEC codes, we focus on rotated surface codes only and achieve nearly 25% reduction in total qubit overhead. We also present a few use cases where the proposed idea enables the usage of higher-distance surface codes at a relatively lesser qubit count. Our analysis shows that the modified approach enables users to achieve similar or better error correction with fewer qubits, especially for higher distances (d ≥ 13). Additionally, we identify conditions where the modified code allows for extended distances (d+k) while using the same or fewer resources as the original, offering a scalable and practical solution for quantum error correction. These findings emphasize the modified surface code's potential to optimize qubit usage in resource-constrained quantum systems.

findings.claim: A proven lower bound says QEC restricted to geometrically local operations in 2D carries a space overhead that grows with system size, even when classical computation is free and error-free. This is a structural limit on planar, nearest-neighbour architectures.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a theoretical result from one arXiv preprint (not peer reviewed). The abstract gives the asymptotic scaling, Ω(√log(1/δ)), but not the constants or the point at which it becomes practically binding. Overhead 'reduction' claims made for local 2D layouts should be read against this bound.
findings.supporting_excerpt: incurs an overhead that grows with the system size, even if arbitrary error-free classical computation is allowed

findings.claim: Low-overhead qLDPC codes depend on dense, long-range connectivity that is hard to build, especially on superconducting chips. A proposed workaround removes up to 50% of long-range links but roughly doubles syndrome-extraction circuit depth. The connectivity problem is traded for time cost, not removed.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: arXiv preprint with no hardware demonstration in the abstract. Deeper circuits give physical errors more time to accumulate. The abstract says circuit-level distance is 'largely preserved' but does not give logical error rates under realistic noise, so the net effect is a gap.
findings.supporting_excerpt: remove up to 50% of long-range connections while approximately doubling the circuit depth

findings.claim: Headline performance for the new high-rate 'Cornucopia' qLDPC codes is extrapolated, not measured. The logical error rates of 2.6e-16 and 1.9e-31 assume physical error rates of 0.1% and 0.01%. The scheme also relies on reconfigurable neutral-atom rearrangement, so one hardware platform and its control stack carry the result.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Single arXiv preprint (OpenAlex lists 11 citations). The abstract does not report atom-movement time, loss, or the effect of correlated errors on the extrapolation. Those are gaps, not demonstrated failures. The pseudo-threshold of >0.4% is described as comparable to the surface code and bivariate bicycle codes, so the claimed advantage is mainly in rate, not threshold.
findings.supporting_excerpt: achieving an extrapolated logical error rate of $2.6\times10^{-16}$ ($1.9\times10^{-31}$) per logical qubit per cycle, assuming the physical error rate of $0.1\%$ ($0.01\%$)

findings.claim: In trapped-ion 2D crystals, crosstalk between parallel entangling gates raises the needed surface-code distance from 3 to 5. Parallelism, which QEC needs in order to have a threshold, therefore increases qubit cost. The paper reports a break-even point under 'realistic parameters', but this comes from numerical modelling.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: arXiv preprint, numerical only. The abstract treats the 10^-10 logical-error goal as a long-term target and does not claim it has been reached. Whether the 'realistic parameters' match current ion hardware at scale is not checked in the abstract.
findings.supporting_excerpt: a distance-5 code is necessary to correct the two-qubit crosstalk error

findings.claim: Most of the overhead-reduction results in this set come from simulation or numerics, not hardware. They give modest or narrow gains: soft information (up to 11% and 20% better suppression, 13% and 33% fewer physical qubits), flag-sharing on small codes ([[17,1,5]], [[19,1,5]], [[5,1,3]]), and ancilla recycling (~25% fewer qubits in rotated surface codes). Real-device noise could erode these gains.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Judgement across three abstracts. Soft information and flag-sharing are explicitly simulation-based, and the ancilla-reuse paper presents only an analysis. The soft-information paper is an arXiv preprint (also listed with a Quantum Sci. Technol. venue) and the flag-sharing paper is also an arXiv preprint. The abstracts do not show whether the gains hold with real correlated noise, readout limits, or added classical-decoding load. That is a gap, not a contradiction. The flag-sharing 'order of magnitude' pseudothreshold gain is relative to prior schemes for very small codes.

findings.claim: The cost of non-Clifford (T) gates through magic-state distillation is described as a major overhead, needing many physical qubits and complex measurement and feedback. The proposed alternative, a DFS-encoded geometric logical T gate, has only been shown numerically in superconducting circuits. It is not yet a proven replacement.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: arXiv preprint (the abstract is truncated). The abstract's account of distillation cost is the authors' framing, not an independent measurement. The alternative is evaluated by numerical simulation against other gate protocols. Whether it fits inside a fault-tolerant logical stack is not addressed in the abstract.
findings.supporting_excerpt: conventional magic state distillation requires massive physical qubit overhead across successive distillation rounds, alongside sophisticated measurement and feedback control

findings.claim: A non-peer-reviewed Zenodo preprint argues that active QEC has a Landauer thermodynamic floor of (n−k)/k·kT·ln2 per logical qubit per round, and that biology avoids it through structure. Its own code comparison returned a 'partial null', and it is not evidence of a practical energy bottleneck. Autonomous and dissipative correction is named as the boundary of the claim.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: A single zero-citation preprint on Zenodo. Its test is a classical NAND-like flash channel, not a quantum device. The abstract does not compare the floor with real cryogenic control power, so I cannot judge whether the floor matters in practice. The biology analogy is speculative. The paper also defines its own metric (JPCUB), which has no independent validation. I treat it as a possible theoretical constraint to monitor, not an established limit.

hype_flags: 'Ultra-low overhead' / 'low-overhead' codes: the headline logical error rates are extrapolated from assumed physical error rates and rest on simulation, not hardware.
'Defying overhead' (ancilla recycling): the evidence is an analysis on rotated surface codes, with about 25% fewer qubits at most; this reduces overhead but does not remove it.
'Thermodynamic floor' for QEC and the biological 'correction-free' analogy: this is a single unreviewed preprint with a partial null result and classical test channels.
'Error suppressed to the fourth order' for geometric T gates: numerical results only, with no demonstrated fault-tolerant integration.
Overhead 'reduction' framings that ignore trade-offs such as doubled circuit depth, long-range connectivity needs, and decoder or readout complexity.

finding.claim: S1 and S2 present the Willow result as evidence of scalable fault tolerance but leave out caveats from the same abstract. Logical performance of the repetition codes is limited by rare correlated error events, about once per hour (3×10^9 cycles). The result is a memory only, with no logical gates. The real-time decoding result is at distance-5, not at the distance-7 code that supplies the headline 0.143% figure. Λ=2.14 is a modest suppression factor per distance step. The authors themselves say the performance would meet large-scale requirements only 'if scaled'.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The correlated-error floor and the memory-only scope bound how far the findings can be extrapolated. The Science summary omits both.
finding.supporting_excerpt: logical performance is limited by rare correlated error events occurring approximately once every hour, or $$3$$ $$\times $$ $${10}^{9}$$ cycles.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S3 reads as though leakage is solved. The cited demonstration is a distance-3 surface code plus a distance-21 bit-flip code. The abstract reports reduced leakage populations, not restored exponential suppression of the logical error rate in a larger surface code. The 'resolved a key challenge' framing is the authors' own claim from a small-scale demonstration. It is not an independently established result.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract supports a tenfold reduction in steady-state leakage at small code distance. It does not show that leakage no longer limits scaling. Labelling S3 'verified_fact' with medium confidence overstates what the abstract establishes.

finding.claim: S5 calls neural decoders 'a clearly emerging direction' on the strength of one 2026 preprint. The headline gains are simulation benchmarks: up to 49% lower MWPM logical error rate at d≤5 under SI1000 noise, and speedups over specific decoders. On the only experimental dataset, Sycamore, the new decoder merely matches or slightly surpasses an existing dense neural decoder. A trend claim needs more than one non-peer-reviewed paper.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract shows simulated gains at small distance. The experimental result is only parity with a prior neural decoder. This supports a single-preprint claim, not a 'clearly emerging' field-level trend.
finding.supporting_excerpt: SMD reduces the MWPM logical error rate by up to 49% at $d \le 5$ under SI1000 noise
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S6 and S7 are labelled verified_fact, but the abstracts describe numerical or simulation-based work with no hardware demonstration. The hyperbolic-code paper says its codes were simulated. The quantum-autoencoder paper shows learned strategies and 'moderate noise' tolerance with no experimental device mentioned. The 'higher encoding rates and lower overhead' and 'extend logical-qubit lifetime' claims are therefore model-level, and they are not hardware-validated facts.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt confirms the hyperbolic-code results are simulated. The autoencoder abstract likewise reports no hardware run. These findings should be treated as simulation-level, with the 'verified' label limited to 'the authors claim'.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We apply this framework to construct and simulate two representative hyperbolic quantum error correction codes (HQECCs)
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S10 generalises to 'a recurring theme across the review/tutorial literature' from only two sources, and only one of them supports it. The hardware-efficient, continuous-variable, modular superconducting-photon emphasis comes from lecture notes from a 2019 summer school, a specific research group's perspective. The 'For Dummies' abstract is a generic NISQ-era review and mentions none of this. 'Near-term practical directions' is the notes' vision statement and is not a surveyed consensus.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: A single group's lecture-note vision does not make a recurring theme across the literature. The second cited abstract does not corroborate it.
finding.supporting_excerpt: The goal and vision is “hardware-efficient” quantum error correction that does not require exponentially large hardware overhead

finding.claim: General gap: the findings S1–S4 are experimental successes, but nothing weighs the structural cost of scaling them. A proven lower bound shows that locality-limited 2D error correction has a space overhead growing with system size. Alternatives such as qLDPC codes demand hard-to-build long-range connectivity, and routing workarounds trade it for roughly doubled circuit depth. Without this counterweight, the surface-code and bosonic demonstrations may be read as nearer to practical scale than the evidence supports.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The cited lower bound applies to 2D local architectures, and the routing preprint shows connectivity can be traded for circuit depth. Together they show scale-up is constrained by overhead and connectivity. The Science findings do not address these constraints.
finding.supporting_excerpt: in order to operate a quantum error correcting code in 2D at a logical error rate of $δ$, a space overhead of $Ω(\sqrt{\log(1/δ)})$ is needed
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

limitations: Only 12 papers, and only titles/abstracts (mostly abstract_only; some truncated). No full-text methods, noise models or error bars were checked.
Most evidence is arXiv or Zenodo preprints that are not peer reviewed. Several results are simulation-only, so hardware reproducibility is mostly unassessed.

Two items have no abstract (src_0192635a40, a Nature Physics demonstration of low-overhead codes with 67 citations, and src_c9bb5e9898, an overhead calculator). I cannot assess their results or caveats, and I drew no conclusions from them.
The decoherence paper on random Lindbladians (src_67e9b52016) is generic theory on random open systems and only loosely tied to QEC engineering, so I did not use it as a risk finding.

The search was oriented to overhead and so under-covers other risks: decoder latency and classical compute, leakage and correlated errors such as cosmic rays, cryogenic wiring and power, and supply-chain concentration. Absence from this set does not mean these are not problems.
No company-level information was available, so I attribute no risks to specific firms.
Only titles and abstracts were reviewed. Caveats may be addressed in full texts that were not read.
src_3ee790e4ad, src_0192635a40 and src_c9bb5e9898 have no abstracts, so I could not assess or use them. For example, the low-overhead code demonstration could bear on the overhead-related findings.
I did not challenge S4, S8 or S9. S4 and S8 are consistent with their abstracts, and S9 already carries the appropriate preprint caveats.
The review cannot independently check experimental numbers beyond the abstract text.

sources.title: CROSS-HAIR SURFACE CODES FOR QUANTUM COMPUTING [WO2026232094A1]
sources.abstract: Methods, systems, and apparatus for performing a fault tolerant quantum computation using a surface code. In one aspect an apparatus includes a multi-qubit lattice defining a plurality of logical qubits. Each logical qubit comprises a plurality of physical qubits, the physical qubits comprising data and measure qubits, a plurality of X stabilizers and Z stabilizers interleaving the X stabilizers. Each logical qubit in a first subset of the plurality of logical qubits comprises two opposing boundaries that define parallel lines of X stabilizer measurements through the multi-qubit lattice and two opposing boundaries that define parallel lines of Z stabilizer measurements through the lattice. Each logical qubit in a second subset of the plurality of logical qubits is positioned at a respective non-adjacent intersection of the parallel lines of Z stabilizer measurements and the parallel lines of X stabilizer measurements.

sources.title: FAULT-TOLERANT QUBITS VIA MULTIMODE RESONATORS [WO2026231161A2]
sources.abstract: A quantum computing system may include one or more multi-mode resonators and one or more superconducting control circuits, where each of the one or more superconducting control circuits is coupled to one of the one or more multi-mode resonators, and where each of the one or more superconducting control circuits includes a superconducting nonlinear circuit. The system may also include a controller. The controller may create, in at least one of the one or more multi-mode resonators, multiple cat qubits associated with multiple acoustic modes by parametric coupling with at least one of the one or more superconducting control circuits. The controller may also implement, in at least one of the one or more multi-mode resonators, a logical qubit based on the multiple cat qubits through error correction using parametrically- driven interactions with at least one of the one or more superconducting control circuits.

sources.title: HETEROGENEOUS DISKS UTILIZATION IN FAULT TOLERANT STORAGE SYSTEMS [US20260339797A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A system for fault tolerant storage includes a network environment including a plurality of computing devices and a plurality of storage devices. The system includes an orchestrator executing in the network environment and configured to receive a first storage request including a first size requirement and a first redundancy requirement. The orchestrator allocates a first storage capacity according to the first size requirement on a first portion of the plurality of storage devices, a first number of storage devices in the first portion corresponding to the first redundancy requirement. The orchestrator updates a remnant table according to the first storage capacity and the first number, the remnant table including one or more entries, each entry indicating an allocation size and a number of storage devices having unallocated storage capacity at least as large as the allocation size.

sources.title: FAULT-TOLERANT OPERATION OF SERIES-CONNECTED INVERTERS TOPOLOGY [WO2026224503A1]
sources.abstract: A system to operate a series-connected inverter (SCI) in a fault tolerant manner includes a controller that determines an occurrence of a fault in a first inverter sub-module of the SCI and pulse width modulation (PWM) signals are suspended for each of the inverter sub-modules of the SCI. The controller provides a first instruction to disconnect circuit breakers that connect the first inverter sub-module to a machine. The controller discharges a first DC-link capacitor connected in parallel to the first inverter sub-module using a discharging circuitry connected in parallel to the first DC-link capacitor. Based on determining that a charge across the first DC-link capacitor is below a predetermined threshold, the controller provides a second instruction to connect a first mechanical bypass switch in parallel to the first DC link capacitor, and the controller resumes PWM signals for each of the remaining plurality of inverter sub-modules.

sources.title: DECODER FOR AN ERROR CORRECTING CODE [WO2026223892A1]
sources.abstract: The invention relates to a computer-implemented method for decoding error syndromes (3) of a quantum error correction code (1) to obtain a recovery set to restore quantum states encoded in the quantum error correction code (1), wherein the error syndromes (3) are results from measurements of the stabilizers (4) of the quantum error correction code (1) executed on a quantum system comprising a plurality of data qubits (5), wherein the quantum error correction code (1) comprises at least two one-lines (6) corresponding to sets of data qubits (5), wherein a tensor product of single-qubit operators acting on each data qubit (5) of a one-line (6) commutes with the stabilizers (4) of the quantum error correction code (1), wherein at least two one-lines (6) have at least one common data qubit (5), the method comprising the following steps: in a rectification step, determining at least one recovery set indicating the set of data qubits (5) on which a recovery operation is to be applied when executed on the quantum system, wherein when the recovery operations are executed on the quantum system a quantum state outside of the code space is transferred to an encoded quantum state in the code space of the quantum error correction code (1); in a post-processing step, for at least one, preferably each, one-line (6) of the quantum error correction code (1) or symmetric differences of one-lines (6) of the quantum error correction code (1), i. determining if the number of data qubits (5) in the intersection of the respective one-line (6) or symmetric difference of one-lines (6) and the recovery set obtained in the rectification step fulfil a predetermined criterion; ii. if the predetermined criterion is not fulfilled, replace the recovery set by the symmetric difference of the one-line (6) or symmetric difference of one-lines (6) and the recovery set obtained in the rectification step; iii. optionally repeating steps i. and ii. until the intersection of all one-lines (6) or symmetric difference of one-lines (6) and the recovery set fulfils the predetermined criterion; outputting the post-processed recovery set.

sources.title: DECISION-TREE DECODERS FOR QUANTUM LOW-DENSITY PARITY-CHECK CODES [US20260340471A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    One or more systems, devices, computer program products and/or computer-implemented methods of use provided herein relate to decision tree decoding for quantum low-density parity check codes. For example, a system can comprise a memory that can store computer executable components and a processor that can execute the computer executable components stored in the memory. The computer executable components can comprise a graph construction component that can construct a decision tree given a syndrome measurement of a quantum processor on a decoding graph of a quantum error correction code. The computer executable components can further comprise an exploration component that can explore the decision tree by incrementally adding a fault to a fault set to construct a correction for the syndrome measurement.

sources.title: ADAPTIVE CANARY QUBIT SYSTEM WITH REAL-TIME NOISE MAPPING AND TELEMETRY INTEGRATION FOR QUANTUM ERROR MANAGEMENT [US20260340472A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    The technologies described herein are directed towards using spare (unused with respect to active use by a quantum process) qubits as “canary” qubits that are measured, after application of a sequence of gates, to detect whether decoherence or noise adversely affected active qubits used in a quantum processing unit. An adaptive canary qubit system obtains telemetry data from sensors in a quantum system, and uses the telemetry data to update a noise map and rank noisy “hotspot” regions” of the quantum processing unit by noisiness. A canary qubit assigned to a hotspot region has its state measured after application of a gate sequence. If the spare qubit is in an error state, the adaptive canary qubit system reassigns an active logical qubit from that hotspot region to a less noisy region. The system includes a model that predicts placement of canary qubits based on historical telemetry data and prior results.

sources.title: ENHANCED REDUNDANCY IN MIXED-VOLTAGE LOW VOLTAGE SYSTEM [US20260336466A1]
sources.abstract: The subject technology provides for a power conversion architecture having a first power converter configured to receive power from a first power source and supply a first voltage domain, and a second power converter configured to receive power from a second power source and supply a second voltage domain. Each converter delivers power to a respective power path including both a primary load and a redundant load. A third power converter is coupled between the first and second voltage domains and enables bidirectional power transfer in response to fault conditions. This configuration supports fault-tolerant operation in safety-relevant automotive systems, including brake-by-wire, steer-by-wire, and autonomous driving systems, where uninterrupted functionality can be beneficial for maintaining operational safety. By utilizing only three DC-DC converters, the subject technology reduces bill of materials cost, weight, component count, and thermal management overhead. The architecture enables mixed-voltage systems while maintaining compatibility across diverse vehicle platforms.

sources.title: EVENT-DRIVEN FINANCIAL TRANSACTION PROCESSING SYSTEM WITH ATOMIC CONSISTENCY ACROSS DISTRIBUTED LEDGERS [US20260340643A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    An event-driven financial transaction processing system with atomic consistency across distributed ledgers is disclosed. The invention provides a distributed transaction framework configured to synchronize financial transaction execution across multiple ledger networks through intelligent event orchestration and fault-tolerant reconciliation. The system includes an event orchestration engine, atomic transaction consistency module, distributed consensus coordination engine, secure transaction validation layer, real-time analytics engine, and regulatory compliance management subsystem. The architecture enables synchronized transaction validation, rollback recovery, event dependency management, predictive anomaly detection, and real-time ledger synchronization across distributed financial infrastructures. The invention further supports interoperability between banking systems, blockchain networks, payment gateways, and decentralized financial platforms using standardized communication interfaces. Additionally, the system provides secure transaction authentication, immutable audit trails, compliance verification, and intelligent workload balancing for improving operational reliability and transaction scalability. The disclosed architecture minimizes synchronization conflicts, reduces reconciliation delays, enhances distributed ledger consistency, and establishes a secure framework for modern distributed financial transaction processing environments.

sources.title: SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR PHOTOVOLTAIC PERFORMANCE ENHANCEMENT VIA WIND-RESPONSIVE MICROFILAMENTS AND PARTIAL SPATIAL MITIGATION [WO2026224614A2]
sources.abstract: A photovoltaic module assembly comprising a photovoltaic module having a light-receiving surface and at least one elongated wind-responsive filamentary element having a transverse characteristic dimension of less than 1 mm along at least a majority of its free length. The filamentary element is anchored to define at least one unsupported wind-displaceable free length and is configured to produce intermittent, spatially discontinuous contact with the surface, thereby providing partial soiling disturbance rather than full sweeping cleaning. In some embodiments, the element interacts with only a subset of photovoltaic cells, while a remaining untreated subset constrains module or string operating current, thereby reducing reverse-bias stress, hotspot risk, and bypass-diode activation under non-uniform soiling conditions. The assembly is mechanically fault-tolerant such that loss of an individual filament does not create sharp irradiance differentials and may be integrated during module manufacture as a permanent passive performance-enhancement structure.

sources.title: PATTERN-LOCK TOPOLOGICAL BOUNDARY DEVICES METHODS AND APPARATUS FOR LOSSLESS EDGE CHANNELS AND GOLDEN-RATIO TILED SURFACE-CODE QUBITS USING RECOGNITION-PHYSICS PATTERN-CHARGE INVARIANT [US20260340469A1]
sources.abstract: A pattern-lock device includes a first region having a first integer pattern-charge value J1, a second region having a second integer pattern-charge value J2 different from J1, and an interface between the regions. When DeltaJ=J2−J1 is non-zero, the interface supports one or more localized boundary modes. In preferred embodiments, the device includes a spacer selected to support interface localization, and each mode contributes a conductance quantum e{circumflex over ( )}2/h. The interface may be patterned as a routing network or along edges of an aperiodic tiling so that vertices define stabilizer sites of a qubit fabric. Disclosed embodiments further include photonic interfaces, multi-mode bus structures, superconducting hybrids, stacked architectures, controller-coupled systems, fabrication methods, validation methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media storing fabrication and runtime-control packages for implementing and operating the device.

sources.title: SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR TROTTER-BASED UNIVERSAL FAULT TOLERANCE [WO2026222032A1]
sources.abstract: The present disclosure provides a framework that enables the execution of nontrivial logical circuit blocks at once, preserving their global structure. This whole-block approach allows for the direct implementation of logical Trotter circuits—of arbitrary rotation angles—on any stabilizer code, providing a powerful new method for fault-tolerant Hamiltonian simulation within a single code block. At the heart of our approach lies a deep structural correspondence between symplectic transvections and Trotter circuits. This connection enables both logical and physical circuits to share the Trotter structure while preserving stabilizer centralization and circuit symmetry even in the presence of non-Clifford rotations.

sources.title: COMPUTER PROGRAM, QUANTUM COMPUTATION SUPPORT METHOD, AND INFORMATION PROCESSING APPARATUS [EP4826604A1]
sources.abstract: [0001]    An information processing apparatus causes a quantum computer to execute syndrome measurements of each of ancilla qubits. The information processing apparatus identifies, from a decode graph in which vertices corresponding to the ancilla qubits is connected by edges corresponding to data qubits, based on results of the syndrome measurements by the quantum computer, one or more first vertices corresponding to one or more first ancilla qubits whose states have been inverted. The information processing apparatus sets, in the decode graph, a boundary line that divides the decode graph into two regions. Then, the information processing apparatus calculates, based on the number and arrangement of the first vertices located between the boundary line and a logical boundary, probabilities that inversion of the state of the logical qubit has occurred and that inversion of the state of the logical qubit has not occurred.

sources.title: SCALABLE TRAINING OF IMPROVED DETECTOR ERROR MODELS FOR DECODERS OF QUANTUM ERROR CORRECTION CODES [WO2026217118A2]
sources.abstract: One example aspect of the present disclosure is directed to a method for operating a quantum computing system (QCS). The QCS has a set of qubits. The method includes accessing detection event data that includes stabilizers measurements for a set of stabilizers of a quantum error correction (QEC) code implemented, via. the QCS, on the set of qubits. A trained detector error model (DEM) for a decoder of the QEC code is generated. The trained detector DEM is generated by iteratively updating a set of candidate DEMs based on the detection event data and an optimization algorithm that includes an objective. A. quantum algorithm is performed, via. the QCS, based on the QEC code with the decoder configured to use the DEM.

sources.title: FAULT-TOLERANT AI ARCHITECTURE WITH DISTRIBUTED PROCESSING AND AUTONOMOUS TASK TRANSITION [US20260319898A1]
sources.abstract: The described fault-tolerant AI architecture provides a robust solution for maintaining reliability and accuracy in critical AI applications. By leveraging distributed processing, continuous monitoring, probabilistic task success evaluation, and autonomous task transition, the invention addresses the limitations of traditional AI and fault-tolerant systems, which do not evaluate probabilistic task completion metrics, ensuring uninterrupted operation in the face of potential failures.

sources.title: FAULT-TOLERANT TRANSITION TO DRIVER-OPERATED STEERING [US20260316823A1]
sources.abstract: In certain embodiments, a method of transitioning to driver-operated steering of a vehicle includes providing, by a first vehicle system, an automatic steering feature for the vehicle. The method also includes detecting, by a second vehicle system, a fault in the first vehicle system. The method also includes, responsive to the fault, the second vehicle system taking control of the automatic steering feature from the first vehicle system and providing the automatic steering feature for a defined period based on a pre-calculated dataset generated by the first vehicle system prior to the fault.

sources.title: BYZANTINE-FAULT-TOLERANT FEDERATED THREAT MODEL TRAINING FOR ADVERSARIALLY ROBUST AI SECURITY SYSTEMS [US20260312975A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A Byzantine-fault-tolerant federated learning system and method for training artificial intelligence security threat detection models across distributed networks of AI security agents, wherein up to N/3 of participating agents may be adversarially compromised. A PRAF applies geometric median clipping, cosine similarity filtering, and credibility-weighted averaging to aggregate privatized gradient vectors while neutralising Byzantine gradient attacks. Per-agent credibility is dynamically modelled as Beta distribution updated through ground-truth prediction verification. A poisoning detection monitor applies sliding-window Kolmogorov-Smirnov test across federated rounds to detect coordinated multi-round poisoning attacks that evade per-round filtering. A rollback controller provides immediate reversion to cryptographically verified prior model version upon detection, supported by non-repudiation ledger implemented as a hash-chained directed acyclic graph providing complete forensic auditability of the training history.

sources.title: MODULAR PHOTONIC QUANTUM COMPUTER WITH AUTONOMOUS AI CONTROL AND ROOM-TEMPERATURE OPERATION [WO2026210195A1]
sources.abstract: A modular, room-temperature photonic quantum computer with AI-driven fault correction, thermal control, and dynamic scalability. A modular quantum computing system is disclosed, operating at room temperature and built from interconnected photonic qubit modules. Each module integrates single-photon sources, optical waveguides, environmental sensors, and a local AI controller. A global artificial intelligence subsystem coordinates real-time error correction, timing synchronization, and dynamic workload balancing using reinforcement learning. The architecture incorporates graphene-based thermal management for passive and predictive heat control, eliminating the need for cryogenic cooling. Modules are hot-swappable, auto-calibrating, and operable in rugged, non-laboratory environments. This system enables scalable, fault-tolerant, high-fidelity quantum computation through a distributed, self-regulating architecture optimized for field deployment.

sources.title: METHODS AND SYSTEMS FOR SELF-HEALING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE [US20260310497A1]
sources.abstract: An AI Agent Platform implements self-healing within AI modules for fault tolerant task execution. The AI Agent Platform may receive a task and an identification of an intent associated with the task. The AI Agent Platform may execute a specialist module using an object derived from the task and the intent. The specialist module defines a sequence of subtasks configured to implement the task. The specialist module can invoke an agent module to execute a first subtask and analyzes a resulting state of the task in response to executing the first subtask. If the state of the task indicates a failure condition, the specialist module may be executed again using a new object derived from the task and the state of the task to generate a new sequence of tasks that extend from the first subtask. The specialist module invokes a second agent module to execute the second subtask.

sources.title: A METHOD FOR PROVIDING MULTIPLE ROUNDS OF ERROR CORRECTIONS FOR A QUANTUM ERROR CORRECTION CODE [EP4818990A1]
sources.abstract:
[0001]    The invention concerns a method for providing rounds of error corrections for a quantum error correction code comprising the following steps:
- initializing a quantum register with N data qubits and a number R of sets of K ancilla qubits,
- encoding logical information on the N data qubits,
- performing R cycles of operations on the quantum register, each cycle of operations comprising entangling gates between part of the N data qubits with part of a distinct set of K ancilla qubits, and
- obtaining measurements from the N data qubits and from each of the R sets, each measurement being the result of a quantum projection operation applied on the considered qubit and of the readout of the quantum projection, the measurements obtained from the R sets enabling carrying out R rounds of error corrections on the measurements obtained from the N data qubits.

sources.title: Quantum Error Correction Decoding via Block-and-Cycle Feasibility Checking [US20260300797A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Systems/techniques that facilitate quantum error correction decoding via block-and-cycle feasibility checking are provided. In various embodiments, a system can measure a syndrome measurement associated with a quantum error correction circuit and a parity check matrix. In various aspects, the system can identify a logical action caused by an error afflicting the quantum error correction circuit, based on performing block-and-cycle feasibility checking on a first linear system derived from the syndrome measurement and from the parity check matrix. In various instances, the system can correct the error, based on applying an inverse of the logical action to the quantum error correction circuit.

sources.title: METHOD FOR PERFORMING QUANTUM ERROR CORRECTION [US20260300796A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A method for constructing a quantum error correction code based on weight reduced classical code is described herein. When the weight of a row r of the classical code check matrix is above a weight threshold x, the row is replaced with a matrix M comprising a first sub-matrix and a second sub-matrix. The first sub-matrix is constructed such that the i-th column of the first sub-matrix has a weight equal to the i-th element of row r. Each column of the second submatrix having a non-zero even-numbered weight. Each row of the second sub-matrix having a weight of less than or equal to (x−w<1>), w<1 >being the weight of a corresponding row of the first sub-matrix. Then zeros are appended to the end of each row of check matrix besides row r, producing a weight reduced check matrix, from which a quantum error correcting code may be constructed.

sources.title: DISTILLATION-TELEPORTATION PROTOCOL FOR FAULT-TOLERANT QUANTUM RANDOM ACCESS MEMORY (QRAM) [US20260299819A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A distillation-teleportation protocol for fault-tolerant quantum random access memory (QRAM) is provided. The protocol may include preparing multiple copies of a faulty physical QRAM resource state. The physical resource states may then be encoded into respective encoded logical resource states, which can then be distilled into a single high-fidelity logical resource state. The high-fidelity logical resource state may then be quantum teleported to enact a logical QRAM gate, up to a correction which can be computed classically.

sources.title: QUANTUM COMPUTER AND METHOD FOR IMPLEMENTING A LOGICAL GATE USING A MAGIC STATE [WO2026195576A1]
sources.abstract: There is provided a method for implementing a logical T gate on an input logical qubit (26) using a magic T state implemented by a quantum computer comprising a plurality of physical data qubits, wherein the input logical qubit is encoded with at least some of the data qubits using an error-correcting code. The method comprises either: (I) performing the following operations: (i) preparing a first logical qubit (23) in a magic T state with at least some of the data qubits using at least one error-correcting code, and preparing a second logical qubit (42) in a magic S state with at least some of the data qubits using at least one error-correcting code, (ii) after preparing the first and second logical qubits, applying a first logical CNOT gate between the first logical qubit as control and the second logical qubit as target, and applying a second logical CNOT gate between the input logical qubit as control and the first logical qubit as target, (iii) after applying the first and second logical CNOT gates, measuring the first logical qubit in the Z basis to provide a first measurement result, wherein the first measurement is a classical binary result representing a first value or a second value, (iv) measuring the second logical qubit in the X basis if the first measurement represents the first value or in the Z basis to the second basis if the first measurement represents the second value to provide a second measurement result, wherein the second measurement result is a classical binary result; or (II) performing a series of operations involving the input, first, and second logical qubits which performs the function of operations (i)-(v) to otherwise provide the first and second measurement results. The method further comprises: (III) depending on the first and second measurement result, determining one or more logical Pauli gates to be applied to the input logical qubit. There is also provided a quantum computer comprising: a plurality of physical resonators; and a command circuit for sending control signals to the physical resonators to stabilize a plurality of physical data cat qubits; wherein the command circuit is further configured to perform the method of distilling the magic state.

sources.title: PEER-TO-PEER ENDPOINT MANAGEMENT SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR DECENTRALIZED DEVICE SECURITY AND ORCHESTRATION [US20260291995A1]
sources.abstract: The present disclosure relates to a method for decentralized device management and security orchestration across a peer-to-peer mesh network. The method includes deploying a plurality of endpoint agents on corresponding endpoint devices to perform one or more of device discovery, inventory tracking, vulnerability scanning, threat detection, and patch orchestration. The method further includes coordinating communication among the endpoint agents within the mesh network, establishing and maintaining consistency and compliance through consensus validation, and allocating operational tasks based on compute power, resource availability, network bandwidth, and priority. The method applies artificial intelligence models to detect anomalies, identify malware signatures, prioritize patches, and generate remediation recommendations. The method also enables bandwidth-aware synchronization, verifies adherence to enterprise policies, and initiates automated remediation upon detecting non-compliance. The disclosed method maintains operational continuity and coordinated defense even during network disconnection, providing fault-tolerant, autonomous, and bandwidth-efficient endpoint management.

draft.summary: Research on quantum error correction is accelerating sharply: the OpenAlex count rose from 703 works in 2024 to 1,383 in 2025 (+96.7%), and 2026 year-to-date is 3,538 against 945 at the same point of 2025. Patent publications are also rising, though the patent search picks up classical 'fault-tolerant' patents, so that signal is noisy [P4]. The strongest experimental evidence is a superconducting surface-code memory operated below threshold and beyond break-even [S1, S2]. The Risk agent's challenges limit what this shows: it is a memory only, has no logical gates, and the suppression factor is modest [C1]. Structural overhead and connectivity limits remain open [R1, R2, C6]. Company evidence is mostly roadmaps and unverified claims, with Quantinuum targeting up to 100 logical qubits in 2027 [M2] and Xanadu having demonstrated only twelve [M4]. The main uncertainty is whether laboratory below-threshold results can scale to useful fault-tolerant machines at acceptable qubit cost and on a commercially relevant timeline. Research activity is not evidence of commercial success.
draft.plain_summary: Quantum error correction is a way of protecting fragile quantum computers from the mistakes they constantly make, and it is needed before they can do useful work. Scientific papers and patents on it are growing very fast, and one laboratory test showed errors can be reduced as the system grows. The big question is whether this can be scaled up to machines large enough to matter without needing an impractical number of components.

themes.name: Surface-code and bosonic logical-qubit demonstrations moving toward fault tolerance

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Experiments show below-threshold memory, beyond break-even operation, tenfold leakage reduction and beyond break-even qudits [S1, S2, S3, S4]. They are small-scale memory demonstrations without logical gates, and the correlated-error and scale caveats remain [C1, C2]. Vendor claims of logical-qubit milestones are company statements, and the X-reported earnings figures are unverified [M1, X7]. Expect incremental demonstrations rather than useful fault-tolerant computation.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Quantinuum states it expects Sol in 2027 with up to 100 logical qubits, an unverified company expectation [M2]. Both Quantinuum and Xanadu describe fault tolerance at scale as subject to substantial scientific and engineering uncertainty [M5]. Xanadu has so far shown twelve logical qubits and has unresolved photon loss [M4]. The evidence does not show whether these roadmaps will be met.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Quantinuum's Apollo (hundreds of logical qubits, 2029) is a company target only [M2]. The authors of the below-threshold result say large-scale requirements would be met only 'if scaled' [C1]. A proven 2D locality overhead bound and connectivity trade-offs create structural headwinds [R1, R2, C6]. The evidence cannot support a confident long-term view.

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: Below-threshold scaling, leakage control and bosonic beyond break-even results compound into logical-gate demonstrations. Vendor roadmaps to tens and then hundreds of logical qubits are met, and fault-tolerant machines gain commercial traction.

base.label: forecast
base.narrative: Laboratory progress continues with modest suppression factors and small logical-qubit counts. Real-time decoding and leakage handling improve, but scaling cost and engineering uncertainty slow commercial milestones, consistent with company risk disclosures.

bear.label: forecast
bear.narrative: Rare correlated errors, leakage at larger distances and the overhead growth of locality-limited architectures prevent practical scaling. Company roadmaps slip, and demonstrations remain memories rather than computers.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Patent applications concentrate on decoding and detector error modelling [P1, P2], and AMD, IBM and ORNL announced a co-design platform for error correction, an unverified social-media claim [X1, X2, X5]. Reported 20% gains from Riverlane and Quantum X Labs are preliminary and unverified [X3, X4]. ML decoder gains are mostly simulation, and there is only one preprint behind the 'trend' [S5, C3]. Activity is real but the performance evidence is thin.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Real-time decoding at 63 µs average latency has been shown at distance-5 [S2], and patent filings address the decoder bottleneck [P2]. Whether ML decoders hold their simulated gains on real hardware is unproven, since on the only experimental dataset the new decoder only matched an existing one [C3]. The evidence does not show who captures value.

horizons.label: forecast

themes.name: Low-overhead codes (qLDPC, hyperbolic, bosonic) and the scaling-cost problem

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Overhead-reduction claims are mostly simulation and narrow in scope [R5], and hyperbolic and autoencoder results lack hardware validation [C4]. Headline qLDPC error rates are extrapolated and platform-specific [R3]. Expect papers and patents, not deployed low-overhead systems.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: qLDPC codes need dense long-range connectivity that is hard to build, and routing workarounds roughly double circuit depth [R2]. Magic-state distillation remains a major overhead, with alternatives shown only numerically [R6]. Patents describe distillation and logical-gate protocols [P5], but the evidence does not show whether any of this reaches hardware in this window.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: A proven lower bound says local 2D QEC overhead grows with system size [R1], so progress depends on non-local or alternative architectures that are unproven at scale [R2, R3]. The evidence does not allow a confident long-term view.

bull.label: forecast
